Subscribe Close YUMA PROVING GROUND, Ariz. — U.S. Northern Command’s fourth iteration of its large-scale Falcon Peak exercise is designed to demonstrate, refine and connect capabilities that counter small, hostile drones in desert terrains, and for the first time, those threatening America along the southern border. “What we’re trying to do is come up with technologies that help us identify adversary drones and also hobbyist drones, so that we can appropriately — within the bounds of U.S. law and regulation — mitigate that threat both to troops as well as to civilians and facilities,” Northcom spokesperson Becky Farmer said on Tuesday. Officials shed new light about the command’s intent for its ongoing Falcon Peak 26.2 with a small group of reporters who were invited to observe the joint military demonstration as it comes to a close this week. The organized trials cover three lanes: drone-on-drone interceptors, kinetic or ballistic mitigation using shotgun-based systems, and capabilities that sense and detect enemy unmanned aerial systems. Advertisement “You can’t fight what you can’t see, and our commander [Northcom’s Gen. Greg Guillot] says that a lot,” Farmer told DefenseScoop. “So, as you saw today, seeing with your naked eye is really hard, and by the time your eyes see it, it might be too late to do anything about it.” She added: “And so having that capability with our sensors, whether that’s infrared, other optical means, or other technology, the farther out we can see something — and then we can track it and really tell whether that’s friendly or not friendly — is key to this fight.” Pentagon counter-UAS exercises have been known to focus often on tactical, expeditionary warfare and impacts on forces abroad. But this year, Falcon Peak 26.2 is directly targeting Northcom’s mission to defend against drone threats that have been emerging across U.S. airspace, critical infrastructure, and incursions escalating around the southern border. “Cartels use drones for many things, including drug smuggling, human trafficking, and also surveilling our troops,” Farmer noted. “And so we’re here in this environment to test capabilities that we can use against that very specific threat.” (Watch a video about the exercise here ) Advertisement Testing at Yuma replicates conditions along America’s 1,954-mile border with Mexico. “The focus this year is really not only just on counter-drone at-large, but the warfighter who’s [there],” Farmer said. “Being here replicates a large portion of that border. And so we’re really getting after putting the right technology in the warfighters’ hands. Being here in Yuma gets us that much closer.” Beyond being the first Falcon Peak exercise to emulate border combat and unfold on the military’s sprawling Yuma Proving Ground, 26.2 also marks the first iteration that the command deployed Anduril’s autonomous command-and-control (C2) software platform Lattice as a digital backbone and baseline standard against which all commercial sensor-to-shooter counter-UAS assets are measured. It follows a selection by the military’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) of Lattice to serve as a key tactical C2 solution for C-UAS, via an $87 million contract under the Army’s recently-announced Enterprise Agreement with Anduril. “Usually, the customer has a version of Lattice, and they’re bringing in systems to integrate on that. This is the first go-around where the test organization has the Lattice capability and they’re integrating into our infrastructure,” Robert Fletcher, Yuma Proving Ground’s sensor branch team lead, said. Advertisement As he suggested, the commercial participants must feed their sensor data, radar tracks and targeting data directly into the Lattice system during this exercise. At least 20 vendors have been involved, Fletcher said, with anywhere between 15 and 30 opportunities to do intercepts. Lattice offers “the C2 that is supposed to be used to standardize that plug-and-play aspect,” he told DefenseScoop. “So if all counter-UAS can plug-and-play, and that’s what everyone’s using, you can relocate it, buy it, use it — and I think that’s the end goal.” Share Facebook LinkedIn Twitter Copy Link Add to Preferred Sources Advertisement Advertisement More Like This Advertisement Top Stories Advertisement More Scoops Director of Joint Interagency Task Force 401 Brigadier General Matthew Ross tours Yuma Test Center at Yuma Proving Ground in Yuma, Ariz., Sept. 22, 2026, ahead of the Falcon Peak demonstration. Joshua “Spider” Webb 2w Report this post The battlefield has officially moved to our backyard. Incursions by unauthorized, small unmanned aerial systems (sUAS) over domestic U.S. military bases are no longer a rare nuisance—they are an active homeland security challenge. To stay ahead of this rapidly evolving threat, U.S. Northern Command (USNORTHCOM) and JIATF-401 are currently in the dirt at the Yuma Proving Ground, running Falcon Peak 26.2 . This isn't just another exercise. It’s an intensive operational evaluation designed to fast-track commercial innovation directly to the front line of homeland defense. Testing is broken down into three critical lanes: 🛰️ Sensors: Advanced radar, RF detection, and optical suites designed for long-range tracking in austere desert conditions. 🛡️ Interceptors: Solutions that actively hunt and neutralize threats. 💥 Kinetic-Ballistic: Physically downing malicious drones with low collateral damage. Key takeaway for defense tech innovators: The U.S. military is actively looking for rapid-response, deployable tech that integrates directly into military networks (like Lattice for Air Defense and ATEC Data Mesh). If you build technology that can detect, track, and defeat small threats in domestic airspace under FAA constraints, the Department of War is ready to move fast . By Brandi Vincent; 23 Sep 2026 U.S. Northern Command’s fourth iteration of its large-scale Falcon Peak exercise is designed to demonstrate, refine and connect capabilities that counter small, hostile drones in desert terrains, and for the first time, those threatening America along the southern border. “What we’re trying to do is come up with technologies that help us identify adversary drones and also hobbyist drones, so that we can appropriately — within the bounds of U.S. law and regulation — mitigate that threat both to troops as well as to civilians and facilities,” Northcom spokesperson Becky Farmer said on Tuesday. Officials shed new light about the command’s intent for its ongoing Falcon Peak 26.2 with a small group of reporters who were invited to observe the joint military demonstration as it comes to a close this week. The organized trials cover three lanes: drone-on-drone interceptors, kinetic or ballistic mitigation using shotgun-based systems, and capabilities that sense and detect enemy unmanned aerial systems. “You can’t fight what you can’t see, and our commander [Northcom’s Gen. I see this as the strongest signal yet to how defense tech needs to innovate and its implications: Integration and Lethality. This is Northcom's fourth large-scale Falcon Peak exercise, and the first aimed at drone threats along the southern border, where cartels use drones for smuggling, human trafficking, and surveilling US troops. The trials ran in three lanes: drone-on-drone interceptors, shotgun-based kinetic defeat, and sensing and detection, with at least 20 vendors and 15 to 30 intercept opportunities. What’s unique about Northcom’s Falcon Peak 26.2 counter-drone exercise +3 Now let's map it to OODA: Observe / Find-Fix. Northcom's point is that the farther out you detect, track and classify friend or foe, the more options you have. Orient / Track-Target. Operators have to separate adversary drones from hobbyist drones and respond within US law. Overseas the rules are looser. Over American soil, a classification error costs you in both directions: miss the threat, or hit a civilian. Decide. The C2 layer. This is the real news. Act / Engage. Interceptors and shotguns. Cheap effectors against cheap threats. Assess. Closing the loop fast enough to reload the next cycle. What You Need to Know: For the first time, Northcom used Anduril's Lattice as the digital backbone and the baseline standard every commercial sensor-to-shooter asset was measured against, following JIATF-401's selection of Lattice under an $87M contract. Normally the customer brings Lattice and integrates systems onto it; here the test organization owned the capability and vendors had to feed their sensor, radar and targeting data into it. What’s unique about Northcom’s Falcon Peak 26.2 counter-drone exercise +2 That inverts the evaluation model. Vendors are no longer judged on who has the best standalone sensor. They're judged on how much they speed up a loop someone else owns. Three takeaways: For founders: INTEGRATION IS NOW THE PRODUCT. If your tracks don't flow cleanly into the enterprise C2, your performance doesn't count. For investors: value is accumulating in the Orient and Decide layers. Point solutions in sensing and defeat need a sharp edge: better track quality, faster classification, or lower cost per intercept. Whoever compresses the loop wins. The approximately €300 million government order involves Auterion and the Ukrainian company Airlogix, with the first units already produced in Munich and final deliveries expected by mid-2027. The programme represents more than another weapons package. Germany is creating a dedicated production capacity to support Ukraine over time. The delivery schedule also indicates that Berlin is preparing either for a prolonged war or for the continued military reinforcement of Kyiv during and after any negotiation. The aircraft will reportedly use artificial intelligence to operate under intense electronic warfare conditions. Conventional unmanned systems often depend on satellite navigation and radio links that can be jammed, disrupted or manipulated. Greater onboard autonomy could allow the aircraft to recognise terrain, correct their route and continue towards selected targets after losing contact with their operators. Their potential targets include refineries, ammunition depots, airfields, railway junctions and command centres. Their strategic value will not depend only on the accuracy of each individual aircraft, but on the ability to deploy them in large numbers and overwhelm Russian air defences. Quantity itself becomes a military advantage. Relatively inexpensive systems can force Russia to use costly interceptors, disperse air-defence batteries and protect infrastructure across a vast territory. Even if many aircraft are destroyed, those penetrating the defences may cause damage far exceeding their production cost. The programme also reflects a new industrial model. Ukraine contributes battlefield experience and rapid technological adaptation; Germany provides capital, manufacturing facilities, supply networks and protection from direct Russian air attacks. The result could serve not only Ukraine but also the future requirements of European armed forces. However, Europe’s real autonomy will depend on more than final assembly. Sensors, cameras, processors, motors and electronic components are often supplied through global chains, many linked to Asian manufacturers. Industrial sovereignty therefore requires control over critical technologies as well as production plants. The political implications are equally significant. If these aircraft are used against targets deep inside Russia, Moscow will portray Germany as a direct participant in the conflict. The decisive questions will concern targeting assistance, operational restrictions and the degree of autonomy granted to Kyiv. Five thousand unmanned aircraft will not determine the outcome of the war alone.
